derry_potter.text: Welcome to the Craft Village. Mind the wet clay. It is hard to wash out of a good opinion.
In the 1800s Derry~Londonderry became famous for making shirts. Thousands of people worked in the factories, most of them women.
Some streets in the city had a shirt factory at every corner. Now we have pottery, and fewer collars.

then.text: I am going, I am going. Hugh the schoolmaster says it is not the facts of history that shape us but the images of the past that live on in the language. I am paraphrasing. The real line is better, and I am saving it for the stage.

The stage manager sent you? Tell her I was researching. In 1833 the Ordnance Survey came to Ireland with chains and theodolites and wrote Baile Beag down as Ballybeg, and a thousand other places with it. I needed to feel that over a scone.

Friel's trick is that the Irish characters speak English on stage and the English soldiers cannot understand a word of it. The audience does the translating. It is the cleverest thing ever done in this city, and that includes the walls.
Right. Back to the Guildhall. Stephen Rea played Owen on the first night in 1980, you know. No pressure.

else.text: {greeting} An actor, resting, which is our word for a scone. Field Day started in this city in 1980, with Translations in the Guildhall. The best play ever written about a map.
